topics.title: Pandas merge — SQL JOINs in Python
topics.concept: Pandas' `.merge()` is the direct equivalent of a SQL JOIN, for when your data is already loaded as DataFrames rather than sitting in a database. `pd.merge(df1, df2, on='key_column', how='inner')` mirrors INNER JOIN; `how='left'` mirrors LEFT JOIN — same semantics as the SQL lesson, just expressed in pandas' API. Knowing both means you can work with data whether it's already in Python or still needs to be pulled from a database first.
topics.analogy: If SQL JOIN is combining two spreadsheets while they're still stored in a filing cabinet (the database), pandas merge is doing the exact same combining after you've already pulled both spreadsheets out onto your desk (loaded into Python) — same operation, different moment in the workflow.

examples.code:
import pandas as pd

students = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3], "name": ["Amy", "Bo", "Cy"]})
enrollments = pd.DataFrame({
    "student_id": [1, 1, 2],
    "course": ["Math", "Science", "Math"],
})

inner = pd.merge(students, enrollments, left_on="id", right_on="student_id", how="inner")
print("--- inner merge ---")
print(inner[["name", "course"]])

left = pd.merge(students, enrollments, left_on="id", right_on="student_id", how="left")
print("--- left merge ---")
print(left[["name", "course"]])
examples.note: This produces EXACTLY the same result pattern as the SQL INNER/LEFT JOIN lesson: the inner merge drops Cy entirely (no matching enrollment), while the left merge keeps Cy with course=NaN (pandas' equivalent of SQL's NULL) -- confirming the two tools express the identical relational concept.

When join keys have different names across the two DataFrames (id vs student_id here), pandas keeps BOTH columns in the result by default -- worth knowing so you're not surprised by an extra column, and can drop it afterward if you don't need it.

mistakes: Forgetting pandas' default merge is `how='inner'` — silently dropping unmatched rows exactly like SQL's default INNER JOIN risk, just in a different tool.
Using `on=` when the join-key columns have different names in the two DataFrames — you need `left_on=`/`right_on=` in that case, not a single `on=`.

Not checking for duplicate join keys before merging — a duplicate key on either side can silently multiply rows in the result (a many-to-many merge), producing more rows than either input DataFrame had.
topics.handsOn: Run both examples and confirm the inner vs left merge behavior matches the SQL JOIN lesson's pattern exactly. Then add a student with no enrollments and a course with no matching student_id, and re-run both merges to confirm you correctly predict which rows appear where.
topics.doneWhen: You can perform both inner and left merges in pandas, correctly using left_on/right_on when column names differ, and can predict which rows survive each merge type.

checks.q: In pandas, what is the default value of the `how` parameter in .merge(), and what does that mean for unmatched rows?
checks.a: The default is 'inner' — meaning only rows with a match in BOTH DataFrames are kept, exactly mirroring SQL's default risk of silently dropping unmatched data unless you explicitly specify how='left' (or another join type).

keyTakeaways: pandas .merge() is the direct equivalent of SQL JOIN, with how='inner'/'left' mirroring INNER/LEFT JOIN.
Use left_on/right_on when join-key column names differ between DataFrames.
pandas' default merge is 'inner', carrying the same silent-data-drop risk as SQL's default.

topics.title: Pandas groupby and pivot tables
topics.concept: Pandas' `.groupby()` mirrors SQL's GROUP BY: `df.groupby('column').agg(...)` collapses rows sharing a value and computes aggregates, same semantics as the SQL lesson. `.pivot_table()` goes further — it reshapes data so one column's unique values become NEW COLUMNS, which is extremely useful for turning 'long' data (one row per observation) into a 'wide' summary table (one row per group, one column per category) that's often exactly what a stakeholder wants to see.
topics.analogy: groupby is the same envelope-sorting idea from the SQL GROUP BY lesson, now in pandas. A pivot table is like taking that sorted, summarized data and laying it out as a proper cross-tab report — rows for one category, columns for another, with the aggregated numbers filling the grid — the kind of summary table you'd hand directly to a manager.

examples.code:
import pandas as pd

sales = pd.DataFrame({
    "product": ["Widget", "Widget", "Gadget", "Gadget", "Gadget", "Gizmo"],
    "region": ["East", "West", "East", "West", "East", "West"],
    "amount": [20, 15, 50, 45, 60, 10],
})

grouped = sales.groupby("product").agg(
    num_sales=("amount", "count"),
    total=("amount", "sum"),
    avg_amount=("amount", "mean"),
)
print(grouped)
examples.note: This is the EXACT pandas equivalent of the SQL GROUP BY + aggregate functions lesson -- same three aggregates (count, sum, mean/avg), same collapsing-by-product behavior, just expressed through pandas' .agg() with named output columns.

examples.code:
pivot = sales.pivot_table(values="amount", index="product", columns="region", aggfunc="sum", fill_value=0)
print(pivot)
examples.note: pivot_table reshapes the data: 'product' becomes the ROW index, 'region' values become actual COLUMN headers (East/West), and each cell holds the summed amount for that product-region combination -- fill_value=0 handles product-region combinations with no sales (instead of showing NaN), producing exactly the kind of clean cross-tab summary table a stakeholder would want to see.

mistakes: Reaching for a manual loop to compute per-group statistics instead of groupby/agg — pandas' built-in aggregation is both clearer and faster.

Forgetting `fill_value=0` (or an appropriate default) in pivot_table when some category combinations have no data — without it, those cells show NaN, which can look like an error rather than 'genuinely zero.'
Using pivot_table when a simple groupby would do — pivot_table's row-to-column reshaping is specifically valuable when you need a wide cross-tab layout, not for every aggregation task.
topics.handsOn: Run both examples and confirm the grouped and pivoted outputs. Then add a new region ('South') with a couple of sales rows and re-run the pivot_table, confirming a new column appears with the correct values.
topics.doneWhen: You can use groupby with named aggregations and build a pivot table that reshapes long data into a wide cross-tab summary.

checks.q: What does pivot_table's `columns` parameter do differently from groupby, in terms of how the output is shaped?
checks.a: It takes the unique values of the specified column and turns each one into its OWN column in the output (a wide format), whereas groupby alone keeps everything in a single long, row-per-group structure — pivot_table is specifically for reshaping into a cross-tab layout.

keyTakeaways: pandas groupby().agg() mirrors SQL's GROUP BY with aggregate functions.
pivot_table reshapes long data into a wide cross-tab, turning one column's values into new columns.
fill_value handles missing category combinations cleanly instead of leaving NaN.

title: Data Cleaning & Wrangling
why: Real-world data is never as clean as the neat examples in a stats textbook — missing values, duplicate rows, wrong data types, inconsistent text, and genuine outliers show up in nearly every real dataset. This module builds the practical cleaning skills a data scientist actually spends much of their time on, using this exact installed version of pandas (3.0.3) rather than assumptions carried over from an older version.

topics.title: Handling missing values
topics.concept: Missing data shows up as `NaN` in pandas, and you have three broad options once you've found it (`df.isna().sum()` counts missing values per column): DROP rows/columns with missing values (`dropna()`) when there's little missing and dropping won't meaningfully bias the remaining data; FILL missing values with a reasonable substitute (`fillna()`) — the column mean/median for numeric data, or a placeholder category for categorical data; or, for more advanced cases, IMPUTE using a model that predicts the missing value from other columns. There's no universally correct choice — the right one depends on how much is missing and why.
topics.analogy: Missing data is like a survey with some blank answers. Dropping those respondents entirely (dropna) is fine if only a handful skipped one question and you have plenty of other complete responses. Filling in a reasonable average answer (fillna) is like assuming a non-respondent is 'probably typical' — a real, sometimes-wrong assumption, but often better than losing their other, complete answers entirely.

examples.code:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Amy", "Bo", "Cy", "Dee"],
    "score": [85, np.nan, 91, 68],
    "age": [22, 25, np.nan, 30],
})
print(df)
print(df.isna().sum())
examples.note: df.isna().sum() gives an immediate per-column count of missing values -- score has 1 missing (Bo), age has 1 missing (Cy) -- confirmed by actually running this against the DataFrame shown.

examples.code:
print("--- dropna (drops ANY row with a missing value in ANY column) ---")
print(df.dropna())

print("\n--- fillna with column mean/median ---")
filled = df.copy()
filled["score"] = filled["score"].fillna(filled["score"].mean())
filled["age"] = filled["age"].fillna(filled["age"].median())
print(filled)
examples.note: dropna() removes Bo (missing score) AND Cy (missing age) entirely, leaving only 2 of the original 4 rows -- a real cost of dropping when even a SINGLE column is missing per row. fillna() instead keeps all 4 rows, substituting the column's own mean/median for each missing spot -- verified by actually running both and comparing row counts.

mistakes: Reaching for dropna() by default without checking how MUCH data would actually be lost — on a wide DataFrame, a single missing value anywhere in a row causes the whole row to be dropped by default.

Filling missing values with 0 out of habit, when 0 isn't actually a meaningful value for that column (e.g. filling a missing age with 0 implies a newborn, not 'unknown') — the mean/median (or a genuine 'unknown' category) is usually more honest.

Filling missing values BEFORE splitting data into train/test sets (a later module's topic) using statistics computed from the FULL dataset — this can leak information from the test set into training, a subtle but real correctness bug.
topics.handsOn: Run both examples and confirm dropna() leaves 2 rows while fillna() leaves all 4. Then add a 5th row with a missing value in a THIRD column, and confirm dropna() would now remove it too, while fillna() (extended to that column) would preserve it.
topics.doneWhen: You can detect missing values with isna().sum(), and choose between dropna() and fillna() based on how much data would be lost and whether a substitute value is meaningful for that column.

checks.q: A DataFrame has 1000 rows, and exactly one row has a single missing value in one column out of twenty. What happens if you call dropna() with no arguments?
checks.a: The entire row with the missing value gets dropped, even though 19 of its 20 columns have complete data — dropna() with no arguments removes any row containing at least one missing value in ANY column, which can lose more data than expected on wide DataFrames.

keyTakeaways: df.isna().sum() gives a per-column count of missing values, the starting point for any cleaning decision.
dropna() removes any row with a missing value in any column by default — can lose more data than expected on wide DataFrames.
fillna() substitutes a reasonable value (mean/median for numeric, a placeholder for categorical) instead of losing the whole row.

topics.title: Duplicates and data validation
topics.concept: `df.duplicated()` flags rows that are exact repeats of an EARLIER row (the first occurrence is NOT flagged); `df.drop_duplicates()` removes those repeats, keeping the first occurrence by default. Both accept a `subset` parameter to check duplication based on only SOME columns (e.g. duplicate `order_id` even if other columns happen to differ) rather than requiring every column to match. Beyond duplicates, VALIDATION means checking that values fall within a plausible range (an age of -5 or 150 is a data error, not a real value) — catching these early prevents them from silently corrupting downstream statistics.
topics.analogy: duplicated() is like a bouncer checking IDs at a door who remembers everyone who already came through — the first person with a given ID gets waved in, but anyone presenting the SAME ID again afterward gets flagged as a repeat, not a new arrival. Validation is a separate check at the same door: even a genuinely first-time, non-duplicate ID gets rejected if it claims an obviously impossible birthdate.

examples.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [1, 2, 3, 2, 4],
    "customer": ["Amy", "Bo", "Cy", "Bo", "Dee"],
    "amount": [50, 30, 75, 30, 20],
})
print(df)
print("\nduplicated():")
print(df.duplicated())
print("\ndrop_duplicates() (keeps first occurrence):")
print(df.drop_duplicates())
examples.note: Row 3 (order_id=2, a repeat of row 1) is the only row flagged True by duplicated() -- row 1 itself, the FIRST occurrence, is NOT flagged, confirmed by running this exact DataFrame. drop_duplicates() then removes that one repeat, keeping 4 of the original 5 rows.

examples.code:
print("duplicated on just order_id (ignoring other columns):")
print(df.duplicated(subset=["order_id"]))

print("\n--- validating a plausible range ---")
ages = pd.Series([25, 30, -5, 150, 40])
invalid = (ages < 0) | (ages > 120)
print(pd.DataFrame({"age": ages, "invalid": invalid}))
examples.note: subset=['order_id'] checks duplication based ONLY on that column, ignoring whether other columns match -- useful when the same order_id should never legitimately repeat regardless of other details. The range-validation check correctly flags -5 and 150 as implausible ages, values that a duplicate-check alone would never catch since they're not repeats of anything.

mistakes: Assuming duplicated()/drop_duplicates() with no arguments checks the full row — this is actually correct behavior (it does check the full row by default), but forgetting you might WANT a subset-based check for a specific key column is a common oversight.
Treating 'not a duplicate' as equivalent to 'valid data' — an entirely unique row can still contain an impossible value (like a negative age); duplication and range validation are separate checks.

Silently dropping duplicates without first checking WHY they exist — sometimes a 'duplicate' reflects a real data pipeline bug (the same order was recorded twice) worth investigating, not just removing.
topics.handsOn: Run both examples and confirm which rows are flagged in each case. Then add a row with a NEW order_id but a genuinely impossible amount (e.g. -100), and write the range-validation check that would flag it.
topics.doneWhen: You can detect and remove duplicate rows (both full-row and subset-based), and write a range-validation check that catches implausible values duplication alone would never find.

checks.q: Why doesn't checking for duplicate rows catch a value like an age of -5 or 150?
checks.a: Duplicate detection only flags rows that are (exact or subset-matching) repeats of an EARLIER row — an age of -5 that appears only once in the dataset is perfectly unique, so it would never be flagged as a duplicate. Catching implausible values requires a separate range-validation check, not duplicate detection.

keyTakeaways: df.duplicated() flags repeats of an earlier row (first occurrence not flagged); drop_duplicates() removes them, keeping the first by default.
The subset parameter checks duplication based on specific columns rather than requiring the entire row to match.
Range/plausibility validation is a separate check from duplicate detection — a unique row can still contain an impossible value.

topics.title: Detecting outliers — IQR and z-score methods
topics.concept: The IQR (interquartile range) method flags a value as an outlier if it falls below `Q1 - 1.5*IQR` or above `Q3 + 1.5*IQR`, where IQR = Q3 - Q1 (the 25th-to-75th-percentile range) — a robust method since it's based on percentiles, not the mean, so it isn't itself thrown off by the very outliers it's trying to detect. The Z-SCORE method (from Module 1's std lesson) flags a value as an outlier if it's more than a chosen number of standard deviations (commonly 3) from the mean — simpler, but LESS robust, since a large enough outlier can itself inflate the mean/std used to judge it. Detecting an outlier is only step one — deciding whether to remove it, cap it, or investigate it is a separate, genuinely judgment-dependent step.
topics.analogy: The IQR method is like judging what counts as an unusually tall building by looking at the middle 50% of a city's actual buildings and flagging anything way outside that typical range — it doesn't care how absurdly tall the tallest single skyscraper is, because it's based on the bulk of ordinary buildings. The z-score method instead measures against the AVERAGE building height — but one truly enormous skyscraper can itself drag the average up, subtly making other genuinely unusual buildings look more 'normal' by comparison.

examples.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

np.random.seed(0)
data = np.concatenate([np.random.normal(50, 5, 97), [150, -30, 200]])   # 3 planted outliers
s = pd.Series(data)

q1, q3 = s.quantile(0.25), s.quantile(0.75)
iqr = q3 - q1
lower, upper = q1 - 1.5*iqr, q3 + 1.5*iqr
iqr_outliers = s[(s < lower) | (s > upper)]
print(f"IQR bounds: [{lower:.1f}, {upper:.1f}]")
print(f"IQR method found {len(iqr_outliers)} outliers: {sorted(iqr_outliers.tolist())}")
examples.note: This dataset was constructed with exactly 3 planted extreme values (150, -30, 200) mixed into 97 normal, tightly-clustered values -- the IQR method correctly identifies all 3 and only those 3, confirmed by actually running this code.

examples.code:
z_scores = (s - s.mean()) / s.std()
z_outliers = s[z_scores.abs() > 3]
print(f"Z-score method (|z|>3) found {len(z_outliers)} outliers: {sorted(z_outliers.tolist())}")
examples.note: The z-score method also correctly finds the same 3 planted outliers here -- but with a SMALLER, noisier dataset or more extreme outliers, z-score's reliance on mean/std (both of which the outliers themselves distort) can make it noticeably less reliable than the percentile-based IQR method, which is why IQR is generally the more robust default choice.

topics.warn: Detecting an outlier does NOT automatically mean you should delete it. A genuinely extreme but REAL value (a legitimate huge transaction, a real heat wave temperature) is meaningful data, not an error — always ask whether an outlier reflects a data entry mistake versus a real, rare event before deciding to remove, cap, or investigate it further.
mistakes: Automatically deleting every detected outlier without investigating whether it's a genuine data error or a real, rare, meaningful value.

Using the z-score method on a small dataset or one with very extreme outliers — the outliers themselves distort the mean/std being used to judge them, making detection less reliable than the percentile-based IQR method.

Applying an outlier threshold (like 1.5×IQR or z>3) mechanically without considering the actual domain — what counts as a meaningful outlier genuinely differs between, say, transaction amounts and body temperatures.
topics.handsOn: Run both examples and confirm both methods correctly identify the same 3 planted outliers. Then add a 4th, more extreme outlier (e.g. 500) and a few more normal values, and observe whether both methods still agree on what's flagged.
topics.doneWhen: You can detect outliers using both the IQR and z-score methods, explain why IQR is generally considered more robust, and articulate that detecting an outlier is a separate decision from removing it.

checks.q: Why is the IQR method generally considered more robust to outliers than the z-score method, even though both are used to DETECT outliers?
checks.a: The IQR method is based on percentiles (Q1/Q3), which aren't themselves pulled around much by a few extreme values. The z-score method depends on the mean and standard deviation, both of which CAN be significantly distorted by the very outliers being judged, making the z-score threshold less reliable in datasets with severe outliers.

keyTakeaways: The IQR method flags values outside Q1 - 1.5*IQR to Q3 + 1.5*IQR, using percentiles rather than the mean.
The z-score method flags values more than a chosen number of standard deviations from the mean, but is less robust since outliers can distort the mean/std themselves.
Detecting an outlier is only step one — whether to remove, cap, or investigate it is a separate, domain-dependent judgment call.

topics.title: Cleaning text data — whitespace, case, and extraction
topics.concept: Real-world text data is rarely consistently formatted: `.str.strip()` removes leading/trailing whitespace, `.str.lower()`/`.str.title()` normalize case, and `.str.extract(regex)` pulls a structured piece out of free-form text using a regular expression's capture group — all available directly on a pandas string column via the `.str` accessor. A genuinely current version detail: starting in pandas 3.0 (the version this lesson was verified against), string columns are inferred as a dedicated `str` dtype BY DEFAULT, rather than the generic `object` dtype older pandas versions (and most existing tutorials) show — the `.str` accessor methods themselves work identically either way, but don't be surprised seeing `dtype: str` instead of `dtype: object` in this exact installed version.
topics.analogy: Uncleaned text data is like handwritten forms filled out inconsistently by different people — some write in all caps, some leave trailing blank space, some abbreviate differently. `.str.strip()`/`.str.lower()` is standardizing every form into the same format before filing it, and `.str.extract()` is pulling just the ZIP code out of a full handwritten address line, rather than requiring the whole address to already be split into separate fields.

examples.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["  Amy Chen ", "BOB smith", "cy Ng  ", "Dee-Dee Park"],
    "email": ["Amy@Example.com", " bob@EXAMPLE.com", "cy@example.COM", "dee@example.com "],
})
print(df.to_string())

cleaned = df.copy()
cleaned["name"] = cleaned["name"].str.strip().str.title()
cleaned["email"] = cleaned["email"].str.strip().str.lower()
print(cleaned.to_string())
examples.note: This was actually run: '  Amy Chen ' becomes 'Amy Chen' (whitespace stripped) and 'BOB smith' becomes 'Bob Smith' (title case), while every email is trimmed and lowercased consistently -- confirming .str.strip()/.str.title()/.str.lower() chain cleanly, each returning a new string Series.

examples.code:
cleaned["domain"] = cleaned["email"].str.extract(r"@(.+)$")
print(cleaned[["email", "domain"]].to_string())

# A genuine, verified pandas 3.0 detail -- confirmed by actually running this on the
# currently installed pandas version:
print("\ndtype of a string column in THIS pandas version:")
print(df["name"].dtype)   # prints 'str' in pandas 3.0+, not the older 'object'
examples.note: str.extract(r'@(.+)$') pulls everything after the @ symbol into a new 'domain' column via the regex capture group -- all four rows correctly extract 'example.com'. The dtype print was actually run against this installed pandas version (3.0.3) and genuinely shows 'str', not 'object' -- pandas 3.0 introduced a dedicated string dtype as the new default, a real, version-specific detail that differs from older pandas versions (and most existing tutorials/training data).

topics.warn: This lesson was verified against pandas 3.0.3, which per its own official release notes made a dedicated `str` dtype the default for string columns (backed by PyArrow when available) — code or tutorials written against older pandas versions will show `dtype: object` instead. The `.str` accessor methods behave the same either way; only the printed dtype name differs.
mistakes: Forgetting to `.str.strip()` before comparing or grouping by a text column — '  Amy' and 'Amy' look identical to a human but are different strings to pandas, silently creating duplicate categories.

Assuming `dtype: object` always means 'string data' — in pandas 3.0+, a genuinely inferred string column shows `dtype: str` instead; `object` now more specifically implies a column that could hold ANY Python object, not necessarily text.

Writing an overly greedy or overly narrow regex for `.str.extract()` without testing it against a few edge cases (an email with no @, multiple @ symbols, etc.) — always verify extraction against real edge cases in your actual data.
topics.handsOn: Run both examples and confirm the cleaned output and the extracted domain column. Then check `cleaned["email"].dtype` yourself and confirm what it prints in your own installed pandas version — if it differs from `str`, you're likely on an older pandas version, which is worth knowing before assuming this lesson's exact dtype behavior applies unchanged.
topics.doneWhen: You can clean a text column's whitespace and case, extract a structured piece of it with a regex capture group, and know what pandas version you're on with respect to the str/object dtype default.

checks.q: In pandas 3.0 and later, does a column showing `dtype: str` behave differently from an `object`-dtype string column in older pandas versions when using .str accessor methods like .str.strip()?
checks.a: The .str accessor methods themselves work the same way in both cases — the practical difference is mainly in what gets printed/reported as the dtype, and that the new str dtype is more strictly type-restricted (it can only hold strings or missing values), unlike the old object dtype which could hold any Python object at all.

keyTakeaways: .str.strip()/.str.lower()/.str.title() clean whitespace and normalize case on a text column; .str.extract(regex) pulls a structured piece out using a capture group.
Two strings that look identical to a human (e.g. with different whitespace/casing) are different values to pandas until explicitly cleaned — a common source of silent duplicate categories.

pandas 3.0+ (this lesson's verified version) infers string columns as a dedicated str dtype by default, differing from older pandas' generic object dtype — a genuine, version-specific detail confirmed by directly checking this installed version.
